# A complete signed-area bound in the two-cell trapezoid

Let

    H={(x,y):0<=y<=1, 0<=x<=3-y},
    D_H={(x,y):0<=y<=1, 1<=x<=2-y}.

For every compact convex Q subset H,

    |Q|-3|Q intersect D_H|<=1.                    (1)

This also proves the desired triangle signed-area inequality for every
convex Q that does not contain the triangle centroid in its interior. The remaining interior case is proved by the shortest-ray lemma in
`candidate c5127f255244bd3c`, which uses the profile result below.

## 1. Exact horizontal compression

The horizontal sections of Q have lengths w(y), on an interval
I=[a,b] subset [0,1]. For positive-area Q, w is concave, nonnegative,
and upper semicontinuous on I; w(y)<=3-y. Replacing each section by
[0,w(y)] gives a compact convex subset of H of the same area.

An interval of length w inside [0,3-y] overlaps [1,2-y] in length at
least min(1-y,(w-1)_+): if it meets both outer intervals, it contains
the whole middle interval; otherwise its positive portion has length
at most one. The interval [0,w] attains this lower bound. Consequently
this compression cannot decrease the left side of (1).

It remains to prove, for every such concave width profile,

    integral_I [w-3(w-1)_+ +3(w+y-2)_+]dy <=1.     (2)

The profile assertion also applies to arbitrary bounded concave w on
an interval I, even if I is half open or its endpoint values are not
upper semicontinuous: close I and replace endpoint values by the finite
one-sided limits from its interior. Concavity, nonnegativity, and the
affine roof bound pass to these limits, and no integral changes. If I
has length zero, the asserted integral bound is immediate.

If Q has area zero, (1) is immediate. Hence assume the positive-area
case below.

## 2. Separate the missing square area

Put w=0 outside I solely for the following integrals (no concavity of
this extension is claimed), and write u=w-1. Set

    V=integral_0^1 (-u)_+ dy,
    U=integral_0^1 u_+ dy,
    A=integral_0^1 (u+y-1)_+ dy.

The integral in (2) is

    1-V-2U+3A.

Thus it suffices to show

    F:=-2U+3A <= V.                              (3)

The set where u(y)+y-1>0 is an interval because u is concave on I.
If it is empty, F<=0 and (3) follows. Otherwise write its left endpoint
as t and its right endpoint as r. Endpoint values do not affect the
integrals. In particular 0<=t<r<=1.

If t=a, the cap interval begins at the left endpoint of the projection.
On that interval u<=2-y, so the integrand contributing to F is
u-3(1-y)<=2y-1; outside it the contribution is nonpositive. Hence

    F<=integral_a^r (2y-1)dy
      <=max(0,integral_a^1 (2y-1)dy)
      =a(1-a)<=a<=V.

The middle inequality holds because the primitive is convex in r.
The final inequality follows because w=0 on [0,a). This handles t=a,
including a=t=0.

Assume henceforth t>a. Continuity of a concave width in the interior
of I gives u(t)=1-t>0. Let c be the left endpoint of the interval
where u>=0. If u(a)>=0 set c=a. Then a<=c<t and u>=0 on [c,t].
If c>a, continuity gives u(c)=0. If c=a, one may have u(c)>0.
Define

    B=1-c>0, L=t-c>0, m=(1-t)/(t-c)=(B-L)/L>0.

In particular L=B/(m+1).

Concavity and u(c)>=0 imply the two inequalities

    u(y)>=m(y-c)       for c<=y<=t,
    u(y)<=m(y-c)       for t<=y<=r.

For the second, the secant slope after t is at most the slope from c
to t, which is no greater than m. The global containment also gives
u(y)<=2-y.

The interval [c,t] therefore contributes at most -mL^2 to F. On the
cap interval [t,r] its integrand is bounded above by

    f(y)=min(m(y-c),2-y)-3+3y.

This is an increasing function, being the minimum of two increasing
affine functions (of slopes m+3 and 2). Consequently its integral from
t to any r<=1 is at most the maximum of zero and its integral to one.
All other contributions to F are nonpositive. It follows that

    F<=max(0,F_full),
    F_full=-mL^2+integral_t^1 f(y)dy.             (4)

## 3. Exact evaluation of the upper bound

The two affine parts of the minimum meet at

    y_*=c+L+L/B.

Thus y_*<=1 exactly when m>=1/B. Direct integration gives

    F_full=(2cBm-1)/(2(m+1))        if m>=1/B,    (5)
    F_full=B^2 m(m-2)/(2(m+1))     if m<=1/B.    (6)

These formulas agree when m=1/B. They also follow by integrating an
affine function with initial value -2(1-t) at t, splitting at y_* when
it belongs to [t,1]. All variables in (5)-(6) were defined above; no
optimization or numerical approximation is used.

## 4. The missing square area pays this bound

We always have

    V>=V_0:=integral_0^c min(1,m(c-y))dy
      =mc^2/2                 if mc<=1,
      =c-1/(2m)               if mc>=1.          (7)

If c=a, the missing projection gives V>=c>=V_0 directly. Otherwise
u(c)=0, and concavity gives u(y)<=m(y-c) for a<=y<c. Thus the deficit
1-w(y)=-u(y) is at least m(c-y) on that portion. Before the projection,
the deficit equals one. If m(c-y)>1, that y cannot be inside the
projection, since it would force w(y)<0. Combining these observations
proves (7), including endpoint cases.

Consider first (5). If mc<=1, subtraction and multiplication by the
positive denominator 2(m+1) give

    2(m+1)(V_0-F_full)
      =(mc-1)^2+3mc^2>=0.

If mc>=1, the corresponding identity is

    2m(m+1)(V_0-F_full)
      =2(mc)^2+2mc-1>0.

Therefore V>=max(0,F_full) in this case.

For (6), there is nothing to prove when m<=2, because F_full<=0.
When m>2, the condition mB<=1 implies

    mc=m(1-B)>=m-1>1.

So V_0=c-1/(2m)>1/(2m). At the same time B^2 m^2<=1 gives

    F_full<= (m-2)/(2m(m+1)) <1/(2m)<V_0.

This proves V>=max(0,F_full) in every case. Together with (4) it proves
(3), then (2), and finally (1).

## 5. Consequence unless the centroid is interior

For K={(x,y):x>=0,y>=0,x+y<=3}, let D be the three centroid-cap overlap
triangles, and let E_i be its three exclusive parallelograms. If a
convex Q subset K does not contain the centroid g in its interior, a
nonzero supporting or separating functional through g is nonnegative
on Q. It is strictly negative on the interior of at least one E_i:
express the functional as sum a_i(lambda_i-1/3), and choose an index i
minimizing a_i. On that cell its value is
sum_{j!=i}(a_j-a_i)(lambda_j-1/3). Every summand is nonpositive and at
least one is strictly negative, because the functional is nonzero and
therefore the three a_j are not all equal. Thus Q misses that cell
except possibly for its null boundary.

Cut Q by the trapezoid spanned by the other two E cells. This removes
only negative area, so cannot decrease |Q|-3|Q intersect D|. An affine
symmetry identifies this trapezoid and its negative triangle with H
and D_H above. Thus (1) proves

    |Q|-3|Q intersect D|<=1=2|K|/9

whenever g is not in the interior of Q. The supporting-separator
argument directly includes g on the boundary and requires no limiting
argument. The case where g is interior to Q is supplied by the shortest-ray lemma
in `candidate c5127f255244bd3c`; that step is independent of the
profile proof here.
